sections.h2: Signs You Need a New Roof in Michigan
body: Michigan is hard on roofs. Freeze-thaw cycles work water under shingles, ice dams back up at the eaves, spring wind and hail storms tear shingles loose, and humid summers bake the protective granules off. Most asphalt roofs in our climate last about 20 to 25 years — and when they go, they rarely fail all at once.

Watching for the early warning signs is what separates a planned replacement from a middle-of-the-night emergency. If several of the items below sound familiar, it's worth having the roof looked at before the next storm.
bullets: Shingles that are curling, cupping, cracked, or missing after a windstorm
Bald spots and piles of shingle granules collecting in your gutters
Water stains on ceilings or walls, or daylight visible in the attic
A roof that's 20-25 years old, or one you know already has an overlay
Sagging areas or a spongy deck, which can signal trapped moisture and rot
Same-age roofs on neighboring homes all being replaced around you

sections.h2: Repair or Replace? Honest Guidance
body: Not every problem needs a full replacement. A few blown-off shingles or a single flashing leak on an otherwise healthy roof is usually a repair. But once the damage is widespread, the roof is past 20 years, or you're paying for the second repair in a single year, replacement is almost always the smarter money.

We'll tell you honestly which camp your roof is in — even when the answer is that you've got a few good years left. Our recommendation goes in writing so you can decide with clear information instead of pressure.

Replace makes sense: age past 20-25 years, widespread curling, or repeat leaks
Repeated repairs on an aging roof usually cost more than one clean replacement

sections.h2: What Goes Into a Proper Roof Replacement
body: A roof isn't just shingles — it's a layered system, and in Michigan every layer earns its keep. We tear off down to the wood deck so nothing rotten gets buried, then rebuild the roof the right way from the deck up. Long roof life comes from the parts you never see.

Ice-and-water shield at the eaves and valleys is the single most important defense against ice-dam leaks, and Michigan code calls for it in those vulnerable areas. Proper drip edge, step and chimney flashing, and balanced ridge-and-soffit ventilation keep water out and let your attic breathe so shingles don't cook from below.

faqs.q: How much does a roof replacement cost in metro Detroit?
faqs.a: Every roof is different, but typical asphalt replacements in metro Detroit run roughly $6,000 to $16,000, depending on size, pitch, how many old layers we tear off, and the shingle line you choose. Larger or steeper homes can run higher. These are typical ranges only — the honest way to get your real number is a free on-site inspection and written estimate.

faqs.q: How long does a roof replacement take?
faqs.a: Most single-family asphalt roofs are torn off and fully re-installed in one day. Larger homes, steep pitches, or complicated rooflines can stretch into a second day. Weather matters too — we won't rush a roof on during rain or high wind. When you book a free inspection, we'll give you a realistic schedule for your specific home.

faqs.q: Should I tear off the old roof or just overlay new shingles?
faqs.a: We almost always recommend a full tear-off. An overlay — a second layer laid over the old shingles — is cheaper up front, but it traps heat and moisture, hides rotten decking, and adds weight your roof carries through heavy Michigan snow load. Tear-off lets us inspect the deck, install fresh underlayment and ice-and-water shield, and start clean.

faqs.q: Can I replace my roof in the winter?
faqs.a: Yes, roofs are installed year-round in Michigan. In cold weather we adjust our methods, hand-sealing shingles and handling brittle materials carefully so everything seals properly. If a leak is already spreading, waiting until spring often means more interior damage. When our schedule allows we can move quickly — book a free inspection and we'll advise you honestly.

faqs.q: Will insurance pay for my storm-damaged roof?
faqs.a: If a wind or hail storm damaged your roof, we can inspect it, document the damage, and work alongside your insurance adjuster through the claims process. To be clear: your deductible is your responsibility, and we never promise free work paid by insurance. We help you understand what's covered and give an honest assessment of the damage.

faqs.q: Architectural or 3-tab shingles — which should I choose?
faqs.a: Architectural (dimensional) shingles are our standard recommendation. They're thicker, more wind-resistant, longer-lasting, and carry stronger manufacturer warranties than flat 3-tab shingles — and they simply look better. faqs.q: How often should I have my roof inspected in Michigan?

faqs.q: Do I need to be home for the inspection?

faqs.q: Will you try to sell me a full roof replacement?

sections.h2: Why Michigan Winters Are So Hard on an Under-Ventilated Roof
body: Metro Detroit roofs take a beating that milder climates never see: heavy snow load, weeks of lake-effect moisture, and freeze-thaw cycles that can swing above and below freezing in a single day. When an attic isn't vented properly, heat leaking up from your living space warms the roof deck. Snow melts near the ridge, trickles down to the cold overhangs, and refreezes into an ice dam that traps meltwater behind it — and that trapped water works its way under your shingles and into the house.

The same trapped attic heat and moisture do quieter damage year-round. Warm, humid air hitting a cold roof deck condenses into frost and drips, which soaks insulation, feeds mold and mildew, and rots sheathing. It also cooks your shingles from underneath in summer, so they curl, blister, and lose granules long before they should. Good ventilation is one of the cheapest ways to protect an expensive roof.

sections.h2: Balanced Ventilation Done Right: Ridge Vents, Soffit Vents & Airflow
body: A healthy attic breathes from bottom to top. Cool outside air enters low at the soffits (intake) and rises out through the ridge (exhaust), carrying heat and moisture with it. The key word is balanced — intake and exhaust have to be matched. We've walked plenty of Detroit-area attics where someone added a ridge vent but the soffits were painted shut or stuffed with insulation, so the roof was quietly pulling conditioned air out of the house instead of venting the attic.
We look at the whole picture and size the system to your roof, then keep the airflow path clear from soffit to ridge so it actually works in a Michigan winter.

sections.h2: Ice Dams: Prevention First, Safe Removal When You Need It
body: The real cure for ice dams is keeping the roof deck cold and even — that means balanced ventilation, enough attic insulation to stop heat loss, and a self-adhering ice-and-water shield membrane along the eaves and valleys during a re-roof. Michigan code and common sense both point to that membrane at the vulnerable edges, and it's your last line of defense when the weather turns brutal.

When a dam has already formed, please don't climb up and chip at it with a hammer or shovel — that's how shingles crack, gutters bend, and people get hurt. Roof rakes and calcium-chloride pucks help from the ground. For a dam that's already leaking, low-pressure steam is the safe way to melt it without harming the roof. When our schedule allows, we can get out to help.

faqs.q: What actually causes ice dams on my roof?
faqs.a: Ice dams form when heat escaping your living space warms the attic and roof deck, melting snow up near the ridge. financing.lead: A roof rarely fails at a convenient moment. When a spring windstorm strips shingles off a slope, or a hard winter of ice dams finally opens up a ceiling leak, the fix can't always wait for the right month to spend. Financing lets you take care of it now and spread the cost over time — so water stops finding its way into your home while you pay at a pace that works for your budget.
body: A roof doesn't wait for a good time to fail, and metro Detroit is especially hard on them. Freeze-thaw cycles crack aging shingles, ice dams push water back under the deck, heavy snow load stresses the whole structure, and spring wind and hail can peel a slope in a single afternoon. Every week a problem sits, moisture works deeper into the sheathing, insulation, and drywall — turning a manageable repair into a much bigger bill. Financing exists so the timing of your repair or replacement is set by your roof's condition, not by whatever happens to be in your checking account that month.

Here's how it works. We work with established third-party lenders who specialize in home-improvement financing. It starts with a free roof inspection and a clear, written estimate — no guesswork about the number. From there, you can apply to finance the work and pay it back in fixed monthly installments. Approval, your rate, and the terms available are set by the lender based on your credit and are offered on approved credit, so we can't promise a specific figure on this page. What we can promise is an honest price up front and a straight answer about your options.

Financing gets you the same quality work you'd get paying any other way: proper tear-off and installation, manufacturer-backed material warranties, and our own workmanship guarantee, handled by a licensed and insured local team. If your roof was hit by a storm and you're filing an insurance claim, a payment plan can also help you manage your deductible or any out-of-pocket gap while the claim is processed — your deductible is always your responsibility, and we never waive or cover it. Ready to see the real numbers? Request your free estimate and we'll walk you through the full cost and every way you can pay for it.
